transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Lee. Thank you for seeing me. Well, it's... it's a bit of a long story, really, because it didn't all just start in one day. I suppose what brings me in is that I just can't seem to get a single moment of peace lately. I keep hearing these voices, and I need to emphasize that they are incredibly clear. 

It started in my apartment—I have this lovely, older place, you know, the kind with the thick plaster walls where you really shouldn't hear your neighbors at all. I've lived there a long time and I know the normal sounds of the building. But I keep hearing women whispering. Not just vague mumbling, but actual, distinct whispering coming from right behind the walls. 

And it's not just at home anymore, which is what really pushed me to make this appointment. I go to the art museum during the week since I'm not working anymore, just to enjoy the quiet and look at the galleries—I've always loved art, I studied it in college, actually. But recently, when I step into those completely empty museum rooms where there isn't another soul around, I hear them there, too. The exact same women. They're always talking about the collections. They whisper to me about which photographs belong in the archive, like they're trying to instruct me on what needs to be preserved or filed away in the permanent collection. It's just so constant, and they speak with such absolute authority about the archives, it's... well, it's very overwhelming when you're just trying to look at an exhibit or sit in your own living room with a cup of tea.
How long have you been hearing these whispering voices—when did they first start?

Well, it hasn't been a quick thing, you know, not like waking up one morning with a cold. It's been a gradual build, but I'd say the voices... and this absolute certainty I have that people are watching my archive, monitoring what I'm doing with the collections... that's been going on for about eight months now. 

Eight months is a long time to live with something like this. It started back in the late fall, right around the time the leaves were really starting to turn, which is usually my favorite time of year. I remember because I was trying to organize my own personal photographs—my own little archive, if you will—and that's when the whispering started to get really noticeable. At first, I thought it was just the wind or maybe the building settling, because old buildings do that, they have their own language. But then it became so clear, so specific about the photographs. And it hasn't stopped since. Every day, for eight months, whether I'm at home trying to sort through my things or at the museum trying to find some peace, they're there, telling me what belongs where and who is watching the archive. It's exhausting, honestly, just eight months of never truly being alone.

Over these past eight months, have you also noticed periods of significantly low mood, loss of interest in things, or conversely, unusually high energy or euphoria, that occurred alongside the voices?

Well, it's funny you mention energy, because... well, there have been these stretches, these really intense periods where I just couldn't stop. I mean, my mood wasn't low at all. If anything, it was the opposite. I felt this incredible, almost electric surge of energy, like I was plugged right into the wall. I would wake up at two or three in the morning, and I wouldn't even be tired. I'd only slept maybe two or three hours, but my mind would be just racing, absolutely racing with all the things I needed to do for the archive. 

I'd be up before the sun, sorting through photographs, cross-referencing dates, making these elaborate filing systems on my living room floor. I felt like I was doing the most important work of my life, really. I was just bouncing from one task to another, completely consumed by it. And the thing is—and this is what's so exhausting to look back on—during those exact same periods, when I was moving so fast and sleeping so little, the voices were right there with me. The women were whispering the whole time, giving me instructions, telling me I was doing it right, or that a certain photograph belonged in a different box. 

And it wasn't just the voices. While I was in this sort of... this whirlwind of energy and archiving, I also had this absolute, unshakable certainty that the museum board was tracking everything I did. I just knew they had someone watching my progress, making sure I was cataloging everything perfectly. So I was racing around, feeling this incredible high, but also hearing the women and feeling this intense scrutiny from the board, all at the exact same time. It was like living in a pressure cooker, honestly, but I just couldn't stop myself. I just had to keep going.
Aside from those high-energy periods, are there times when your mood feels normal or calm—and if so, do you still hear the whispering voices or feel that you're being watched during those times?

Yes, well, that's exactly the thing, Dr. Lee, and it's what makes this all so terribly confusing for me. Because you'd think, wouldn't you, that when the energy finally runs out—and it does run out, eventually, like a clock winding down—you'd think everything else would stop, too. But it doesn't. 

There was this stretch, oh, it must have been a few months ago now, where that electric feeling just faded away entirely. I wasn't waking up at two in the morning anymore. I was sleeping my normal hours, waking up at seven, making my oatmeal, having my tea. I wasn't rushing around making piles of photographs or feeling like I was doing the most important work in the world. I was just... normal. Just my regular self, moving at my regular pace. I even remember thinking, "Oh, good, I can finally just sit in my favorite armchair and read a book without feeling like I have a motor running inside me."

But the peace didn't last, because even though my mood was perfectly calm, perfectly level—I wasn't sad, I wasn't energized—the women were still there. It was actually almost more unnerving, in a way, because the apartment was so quiet, and I was so calm, but I could still hear them whispering behind the plaster. Just as clear as day. And it wasn't just the voices, either. During those several weeks when I was completely calm, I was still absolutely certain that the arts people, the museum board, were keeping tabs on me. I'd look at my telephone on the side table—it's one of those older models, very sturdy—and I just knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that they were monitoring it. Listening in to see if I was talking about the archives. So, yes, even when my mood is completely fine, completely ordinary for weeks at a time, the whispering and the watching... they don't go away at all.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports 8 months of continuous auditory hallucinations (whispering women) and persecutory/referential delusions (being monitored/watched by museum board). During part of this period, she experienced a distinct manic episode—decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, increased goal-directed activity, elevated energy—concurrent with the psychotic symptoms, satisfying mood episode criteria overlapping with active psychosis. Critically, she also had a period of several weeks where her mood was entirely euthymic/normal (no mania or depression) yet the hallucinations and delusions persisted unabated, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur for a substantial period in the absence of a mood episode. This pattern—mood episode present concurrently with psychosis, plus psychotic symptoms persisting ≥2 weeks without mood symptoms, within a single continuous illness episode—meets criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0), rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychosis only during mood episodes) or schizophrenia alone (which would not account for the manic episode).
